notes.meaning: Moses wrote down an official list of the places where Israel camped after leaving Egypt. God directly ordered him to keep this travel record so the people would always remember how the Lord preserved and guided them. Remembering God's past care gives believers courage to face new challenges ahead.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: The early church writer Jerome wrote a study of these forty-two stopping places. He treated them as a picture of the Christian's journey from earth to heaven.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars accept the list as accurate. But they think its neat pattern of about forty sites, one for each year, may show it was arranged to help people remember it. That could explain why some places are left out.

notes.meaning: The Israelites set out boldly from Rameses the morning after the first Passover. While they marched away in plain view, the Egyptians were occupied burying their own oldest sons, whom God had slain. God also brought judgment on Egypt's false gods, proving that the Lord alone has true power.

The people moved from Rameses to make their first stops at Succoth and Etham. Succoth was a place where they set up temporary shelters, and Etham was located right at the edge of the desert. God began their journey one step at a time, preparing them gently for the wilderness.

God directed the Israelites to turn back from Etham toward Pi-hahiroth and Migdol. This sudden change in direction seemed to trap them against the sea, but it prepared the way for God's great deliverance. God sometimes leads his people along unexpected roads to display his saving power.

The people crossed through the parted waters of the sea and walked into the dry desert. After three days of marching without water, they set up camp at Marah, where the water was bitter. God sustained this enormous crowd even through the driest and most difficult ground.

Israel journeyed from Marah to Elim, a welcome desert oasis with twelve water springs and seventy palm trees. This stop provided plenty of cool water and shade for the weary travelers. God provides times of rest and renewal when the road becomes long.

From Elim, the Israelites traveled along the coast and camped by the Red Sea. Following this shoreline route was the only natural path through the rugged mountains of the area. God faithfully guides his people along the path best suited for their journey.

The Israelites moved away from the seashore and entered the Desert of Sin. This dry region lay between the coast and Mount Sinai, where God began sending daily bread from heaven. God meets his people's daily needs even in the most barren places.

After leaving the Desert of Sin, the Israelites pitched their tents at Dophkah and then at Alush. The book of Exodus does not mention these stops, likely because the stay at both was quiet and peaceful. God watches over his followers in quiet days just as much as in times of dramatic miracles.

The camp moved forward to Rephidim, where there was no water for the people to drink. The people grumbled against Moses until God brought water rushing out of a struck rock. God remains faithful and generous even when his people struggle with doubt.

Israel departed from Rephidim and arrived at the wilderness at the base of Mount Sinai. Here the nation camped for nearly a whole year while receiving God's laws and constructing the tabernacle. Taking time to listen closely to God's instructions prepares believers for all that lies ahead.

Leaving Sinai, the people journeyed to Kibroth-hattaavah and then on to Hazeroth. Kibroth-hattaavah means 'graves of craving,' naming the place where many died after demanding meat instead of manna. These site names served as permanent warnings against discontentment and greed.

From Hazeroth, the people moved forward and pitched their tents at Rithmah. The name comes from the desert broom bush, which gave shade and fuel in that area. Many scholars identify this camp with Kadesh-barnea, where scouts were sent out to explore Canaan.

The Israelites departed from Rithmah and set up camp at Rimmon-perez, then journeyed on to Libnah. These sites belong to the decades of desert wandering after Israel turned back in fear from entering the Promised Land. Even during their years of delay, God never abandoned his flock.

Moving onward from Libnah, the community set up camp at Rissah and then at Kehelathah. Kehelathah means 'assembly' or 'gathering,' perhaps describing a spot where the tribes came together. God kept the community together and preserved their families throughout the wasteland.

The camp broke up from Kehelathah and moved to Mount Shepher, and next to Haradah. Mount Shepher means 'mount of beauty,' while Haradah points to fear or trembling. God remains the steady guide of his people through both pleasant hills and frightening trails.

Leaving Haradah, the Israelites pitched their tents at Makheloth and then traveled to Tahath. Makheloth also refers to gatherings or assemblies, likely pointing to a camping spot near pasture or seasonal water. God provided the daily necessities of life across decades of desert travel.

From Tahath, the Israelites journeyed to Terah and then set up camp at Mithkah. Mithkah means 'sweetness,' which likely describes a place where they found sweet water or tender grass for their animals. God often grants his people refreshing moments of sweetness in the middle of long trials.
